strengths: Addresses a genuine practical pain point (expensive per-scene contrastive training) with a fully training-free pipeline, and reports substantial reductions in CLIP feature storage (~1000x) and peak VRAM relative to baselines.

Strong quantitative results: outperforms prior training-based point-level and even several pixel-based methods on LERF object selection (by ~10.7 mIoU) and on ScanNet semantic segmentation across 19/15/10-class settings.

The neutral point processing module (multi-view semantic entropy combined with geometric opacity filtering) is a sensible, lightweight mechanism for handling boundary ambiguity and is validated with a clear ablation (Table 4).

The idea of distilling multi-view CLIP image feature inconsistency into a single canonical textual representation via a VLM (Section 3.3) is a reasonable and reasonably novel engineering solution to viewpoint variance, supported by an ablation comparing it against single-view, averaged, and IoU-filtered image-matching baselines (Table 5).
The paper is generally clearly written and includes useful comparative tables (training time, storage, VRAM) that make the efficiency argument concrete and easy to evaluate.
weaknesses: The central 'polysemy' claim, heavily emphasized in the abstract and introduction (e.g., a desk point being simultaneously 'desk,' 'wooden,' and 'furniture'), is never directly validated by an experiment; no benchmark or qualitative case specifically demonstrates multi-concept assignment to the same Gaussian, leaving this key contribution largely unsubstantiated by evidence.

The framework is a pipeline built almost entirely from off-the-shelf components (SAM, DAM2SAM tracker, Gemini 2.5 Pro VLM, CLIP), so the technical novelty is incremental engineering/integration rather than a fundamentally new representation or algorithm; the object-grouping and neutral-point ideas, while useful, are relatively simple heuristics layered on existing tools.

Reliance on a closed, proprietary VLM (Gemini 2.5 Pro) for the core semantic distillation step raises reproducibility concerns (API cost, version drift, potential non-determinism); despite the claim of being 'VLM-agnostic,' no experiments substitute an open-source VLM to substantiate this robustness claim.

The efficiency narrative ('hours to minutes') is only partially supported: Table 1 reports CLIP feature storage and peak VRAM but omits total end-to-end wall-clock time for the full pipeline (SAM mask generation across granularities, DAM2SAM tracking, periodic re-detection, and VLM querying per object), which could be non-trivial and should be reported for a fair efficiency comparison.

No sensitivity analysis or reported values for the fixed thresholds (τh, τα, η) used across all experiments; given these thresholds directly gate the neutral-point exclusion and query matching, their robustness across differing scene types/datasets is unverified.

Limitations section is brief and does not address potential failure modes tied to VLM hallucination/misnaming at scale, nor quantify how often such errors occur, despite this being flagged as a limitation.

Comparisons are limited to LERF and ScanNet; broader scene diversity (e.g., outdoor/driving scenes mentioned as a motivating application) is not evaluated, somewhat narrowing the demonstrated generality of the method relative to its stated motivations.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practical pain point of existing 3DGS open-vocabulary methods: expensive per-scene contrastive training. The training-free, matching-based paradigm is a reasonable alternative direction.

The neutral point processing idea (using multi-view label entropy combined with a geometric opacity filter to separate true blending/transition points from mislabeled solid points) is a sensible and interpretable mechanism, and the ablation (Table 4) shows both components contribute.

The VLM-based textual distillation strategy for reconciling cross-view CLIP feature inconsistency is a reasonably creative solution to a real problem (viewpoint variance of CLIP embeddings), and the ablation in Table 5 shows a clear, large improvement over single-view/averaged/filtered image-matching baselines.

Reported quantitative results on LERF and ScanNet outperform several recent training-based baselines by a considerable margin, and the efficiency comparison (Table 1) shows large reductions in storage and no per-scene optimization time.
The paper is reasonably well organized, motivates its three claimed weaknesses of prior work clearly, and provides both quantitative and qualitative comparisons.
weaknesses: The 'polysemous' contribution is advertised prominently (title, abstract, intro) as a key differentiator (a point can be simultaneously 'desk', 'wooden', 'furniture'), but no dedicated experiment or metric actually evaluates this capability; both benchmarks (LERF selection, ScanNet segmentation) use single-label queries, so the central claimed novelty is not empirically substantiated.

The pipeline is training-free only in the sense of avoiding per-scene contrastive optimization, but it depends on a heavy chain of pretrained/foundation components (SAM at 3 granularities, DAM2SAM tracking with periodic re-detection, and a proprietary large VLM (Gemini 2.5 Pro) invoked per object). No inference-time/query latency or API-cost comparison is provided, only training time/storage/VRAM, which paints an incomplete efficiency picture and could be a significant hidden cost, especially for scenes with many objects.

Reliance on a closed, non-deterministic commercial VLM (Gemini 2.5 Pro) for generating candidate object names raises reproducibility concerns; results may not be exactly reproducible by other researchers, and no variance/robustness analysis across repeated VLM calls is reported.

There is an unresolved internal inconsistency: the introduction explicitly criticizes Dr.Splat for requiring training of a per-scene feature-compression model, yet Table 1 lists Dr.Splat's 'Scene Opt.' and 'Train Time' as 'None', and the caption claims 'ours is the only method that works directly in 3D without any training,' which contradicts the table's own entries for Dr.Splat.

Fixed hyperparameters (τh, τα, η, top-N views) are used 'for simplicity and robustness' but no sensitivity analysis is provided, leaving it unclear how brittle the method is to these choices across different scene types.

Evaluation breadth is limited to two indoor-focused benchmarks (LERF, ScanNet); several closely related recent works cited in the bibliography (e.g., FlashSplat, Segment-then-Splat, COB-GS, GradiSeg, view-dependent semantics work) are not included as baselines despite apparent topical overlap, weakening the comparison's completeness.

The core back-projection/label-lifting mechanism (accumulating rendering weights from Eq. 1 to assign foreground/background probability) is conceptually similar to prior differentiable 2D-to-3D label propagation approaches used in other Gaussian segmentation works, making this part of the contribution appear incremental rather than fundamentally new.

Failure modes are only briefly acknowledged (SAM mask errors, occasional VLM mislabeling) without quantitative analysis of how often these occur or how they affect final performance, despite the method's heavy dependence on the correctness of these upstream components.

strengths: The paper identifies three concrete and well-motivated limitations of prior 3DGS open-vocabulary methods (expensive per-scene optimization, monosemous assignment, and fragile multi-view CLIP feature aggregation) and designs targeted solutions for each, giving the work a clear conceptual narrative.

The training-free design is a meaningful practical contribution: Table 1 shows dramatic reductions in per-scene adaptation time (hours to none), CLIP feature storage (~3GB to ~3MB), and peak VRAM, which is valuable for real-world deployment.

Strong empirical results: the method outperforms multiple recent training-based baselines (OpenGaussian, InstanceGaussian, Dr.Splat, LangSplat, etc.) by sizable margins on both the LERF object-selection benchmark (+10.7 mIoU over the best prior method) and ScanNet semantic segmentation across three class splits.

The neutral point processing idea (combining multi-view semantic entropy with geometric opacity to identify and discard boundary-ambiguous Gaussians) is a sensible, lightweight mechanism, and the ablation in Table 4 shows both entropy and opacity filtering are complementary and necessary.

The VLM-based semantic distillation strategy (converting volatile multi-view visual CLIP features into a canonical textual representation) is an interesting and well-motivated alternative to naive multi-view feature averaging, and the ablation in Table 5 convincingly shows its advantage over single-view, averaged, and filtered image-matching baselines.

The paper provides fairly comprehensive experimental coverage across two distinct benchmarks/tasks (LERF object selection, ScanNet semantic segmentation) with both quantitative and qualitative comparisons, plus a resource-cost table that contextualizes the efficiency gains.
weaknesses: The central 'polysemy' claim, prominently featured in the abstract, introduction, and title framing (a Gaussian being simultaneously 'desk,' 'wooden,' and 'furniture'), is never directly evaluated. There is no dedicated experiment, metric, or qualitative example demonstrating that the method actually assigns and correctly retrieves multiple simultaneous semantic labels per point; all reported benchmarks (LERF selection, ScanNet segmentation) are effectively single-label retrieval tasks, leaving this headline contribution unsubstantiated by evidence.

The pipeline depends on a closed, proprietary VLM (Gemini 2.5 Pro) accessed presumably via API for generating object identity hypotheses. This raises reproducibility concerns (model behavior can drift or become unavailable) and the paper does not report the VLM's contribution to total pipeline latency/cost, which undermines the completeness of the 'minutes not hours' efficiency claim in Table 1 (only training time, storage, and VRAM are reported, not the full inference-time pipeline cost including SAM segmentation, DAM2SAM tracking, and VLM calls).

The method is a combination of several existing off-the-shelf components (SAM, DAM2SAM, a general VLM, CLIP), and the individual technical contributions (weighted back-projection, entropy/opacity-based neutral point filtering, VLM-based text distillation) are each relatively incremental engineering choices; the novelty lies mainly in the overall training-free pipeline design rather than in a new representation or algorithmic principle.

Two fixed thresholds (τh for entropy, τα for opacity) are used across all experiments, but there is no sensitivity analysis or discussion of how these were chosen or how robust results are to their values across different scene types/datasets.

The comparison set consists exclusively of training-based baselines; no other training-free or matching-based 3D open-vocabulary method is discussed or compared against, making it unclear how this approach positions against any prior zero-shot alternatives (if they exist) versus purely against the training-based paradigm.

The failure/limitation discussion is brief and largely qualitative (SAM mask errors, occasional VLM mislabeling) without quantitative failure-case analysis or error breakdowns, which would strengthen understanding of the method's practical robustness.

strengths: Well-motivated reformulation of 3D open-vocabulary understanding: the 'extrinsic paradigm' that decouples geometry (Gaussian points) from semantics (object-level text indices) directly targets three concretely articulated flaws of the dominant embedding paradigm (geometry-semantic inconsistency at boundaries, storage bloat, and single-vector semantic rigidity/polysemy).

The neutral-point identification mechanism (multi-view semantic entropy + opacity filtering) is a sensible, well-ablated technical contribution for handling ambiguous boundary points, an issue often glossed over in prior work.

Training-free design combined with VLM-based textual grounding of object groups is efficient: the paper convincingly demonstrates orders-of-magnitude reduction in feature storage (GB to MB) and VRAM (Table 1), which is a genuinely useful practical contribution.

Broad empirical validation: LERF object selection, ScanNet semantic segmentation, extensive ablations (neutral-point thresholds, VLM choice, number of prompts, sparse-mask robustness), qualitative editing demonstrations (removal/translation/stylization), and additional real-world/GraspNet tests show the authors stress-tested the method across settings.

Good failure-case and diagnostic analysis (Sec. 9-10), including visualization of CLIP feature inconsistency across viewpoints and quantification of multi-label polysemy in ScanNet scenes, which strengthens the paper's motivating claims with direct evidence rather than assertion alone.
Clear component-wise runtime/VRAM breakdown (Table 9) improves transparency about where computational cost is spent.
weaknesses: Overclaiming of SOTA status on the LERF object-selection benchmark: Table 2 shows several embedding-based methods (LAGA 65.6, 3DVLGS 62.0, Occam's LGS 61.3) substantially outperform the proposed method (54.3 mean mIoU); the paper's claimed '3.9 mIoU' improvement is only relative to the training-free category (LUDVIG), not the overall best baseline. The abstract's statement that the method 'outperforms established embedding-based frameworks' is therefore only partially true and should be scoped more precisely.

The method depends on a proprietary, closed VLM (Gemini 2.5 Pro) for the core semantic grounding step, raising reproducibility concerns; Table 6 shows large accuracy swings (47.0 to 54.3 mIoU) depending on which VLM is used, meaning reported numbers are tied to a specific, non-open model whose behavior may change or be inaccessible to others.

Scalability of the object-level grouping pipeline to scenes with many more objects/instances is not analyzed quantitatively; the reported 9.25-minute processing time is for a scene with 131 categories, and per-object independent tracking, backward matching, and VLM querying could grow expensive for larger or more cluttered real-world scenes (only qualitative, small-scale real-world/GraspNet examples are shown, without quantitative metrics).

Pipeline relies on several hand-tuned, fixed hyperparameters (e.g., re-detection interval Δt=10, τ_area=0.9, τ_iou=0.6, entropy/opacity thresholds) that are fixed across all experiments; while some sensitivity analysis is given for the neutral-point thresholds, the sensitivity of the object-tracking heuristics themselves is less thoroughly justified.

Object editing capability (Sec. 7.3) and real-world generalization (Sec. 7.4) are demonstrated only qualitatively without any quantitative evaluation, limiting the strength of these claimed use cases.

The multi-granularity/polysemy claim, a headline motivation of the paper, is supported mainly by qualitative examples and a post-hoc statistical analysis (Fig. 13) rather than a dedicated quantitative benchmark measuring polysemy-handling accuracy against baselines.

strengths: Clearly motivated reformulation of 3D open-vocabulary understanding: the paper identifies three concrete limitations of the dominant 'embedding paradigm' (geometry-semantic inconsistency, semantic bloat, semantic rigidity) and proposes a decoupled 'extrinsic' paradigm as an alternative, which is a reasonable and non-trivial conceptual contribution.

Strong efficiency gains are convincingly demonstrated: Table 1 shows roughly 1000x reduction in stored CLIP-feature data (MB vs GB) and lower peak VRAM than all embedding-based baselines, with no per-scene optimization required.

Extensive empirical validation across two benchmarks (LERF object selection, ScanNet semantic segmentation) with SOTA or near-SOTA mIoU, plus generalization tests on GraspNet and a real phone-captured scene, lending some confidence that the approach is not overfit to a single setting.

Thorough ablations (neutral point filtering, VLM choice, number of prompts, threshold sensitivity) and an explicit failure-case/limitation analysis (Sec. 9) and discussion of semantic polysemy statistics (Fig. 13) show the authors probed their own method's weaknesses rather than only presenting favorable results.

The empirical demonstration of cross-view CLIP feature inconsistency (Fig. 14) is a useful piece of evidence supporting the paper's core design choice of VLM-based textual distillation over direct image-feature aggregation.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: prompts, thresholds, and implementation details (periodic re-detection interval, IoU thresholds, entropy/opacity thresholds) are reported in the appendix.
weaknesses: The pipeline is a fairly complex chain of existing off-the-shelf heavy components (SAM, DAM2SAM tracking, a proprietary VLM Gemini 2.5 Pro, CLIP text encoder) glued together with multiple hand-tuned thresholds (τh=0.9, τα=0.1, η=0.9/0.9, IoU=0.6/0.9, Δt=10); the technical novelty beyond this orchestration is limited, and the heuristic density raises concerns about robustness and generalization beyond the tested scenes.

The main method depends on a closed, proprietary VLM (Gemini 2.5 Pro) for the critical semantic-labeling step; this limits exact reproducibility and makes it hard to disentangle how much of the reported accuracy gain stems from the proposed decoupled architecture versus simply leveraging a very strong external VLM that competing baselines do not have access to.

Despite an ablation over VLM choice (Table 6), the main comparisons against baselines are not controlled for this advantage—no baseline is given access to an equally strong VLM/image captioner, making the mIoU comparisons only partially apples-to-apples as a test of the architectural idea itself.

Runtime analysis (Table 9) shows the method still takes ~9.25 minutes for a single moderately complex scene (131 categories) dominated by VLM inference and backward matching, and the paper's own discussion notes parallelization was intentionally avoided for memory reasons; scalability to scenes with far more instances or categories is not empirically demonstrated.

The claimed 'multi-granularity, overlapping' object grouping for handling polysemy is implemented simply by running SAM independently at three fixed granularities, without an explicit mechanism to ensure consistency or non-redundancy across granularities; the polysemy claim is largely illustrated qualitatively (Fig. 13) rather than evaluated with a dedicated quantitative benchmark.

Evaluation breadth is somewhat narrow: experiments are essentially limited to indoor tabletop/room scenes (LERF, ScanNet, GraspNet, one phone-captured office scene); there is no evaluation on larger-scale, outdoor, or more cluttered/dynamic scenes where the tracking-based mask-association pipeline (DAM2SAM) might be more failure-prone.

The paper's own failure-case analysis (Fig. 12, Sec. 9) acknowledges that inaccurate initial masks and VLM misclassification directly propagate to segmentation errors, and the method offers no principled recovery mechanism beyond noting this as 'future work,' suggesting the robustness claims should be read cautiously.

strengths: Presents a clear and well-motivated paradigm shift ("extrinsic" vs "embedding") for open-vocabulary 3D Gaussian Splatting, decoupling geometry from semantics rather than injecting high-dimensional CLIP features directly into Gaussians.

Strong practical benefits are demonstrated: elimination of per-scene contrastive training, ~1000x reduction in feature storage (GB to MB), and substantially lower peak VRAM (Table 1), which is a meaningful engineering contribution even independent of accuracy gains.

Comprehensive empirical validation across two benchmarks (LERF object selection and ScanNet semantic segmentation) with consistent SOTA or near-SOTA mIoU results (Tables 2 and 3), plus qualitative comparisons showing sharper boundaries versus OpenGaussian/InstanceGaussian/Dr.Splat.

The neutral-point identification mechanism (entropy + opacity filtering) is a sensible, well-ablated solution to a genuine and under-addressed problem (semantic ambiguity at object boundaries), with clear quantitative gains (Table 4) and sensitivity analysis in the appendix.

Extensive supplementary analyses (VLM choice ablation, prompt-count ablation, threshold sensitivity, sparse-mask robustness, runtime breakdown, real-world/Grasp-Net qualitative tests, failure case analysis, and an interesting analysis of CLIP feature inconsistency across viewpoints) substantially strengthen the credibility and thoroughness of the evaluation.

The multi-granularity, overlapping object grouping naturally supports polysemy (a Gaussian belonging to multiple semantic groups), which is empirically supported by the category-distribution analysis in Fig. 13, addressing a real limitation of prior single-feature-per-Gaussian approaches.
Demonstrated downstream applications (object removal, translation, stylization) show practical usefulness beyond segmentation/selection benchmarks.
weaknesses: The pipeline is fairly complex and depends on multiple off-the-shelf components (SAM, DAM2SAM tracker, a VLM such as Gemini 2.5 Pro, CLIP text encoder). Performance is explicitly shown to be tightly coupled to the underlying VLM quality (Table 6, mIoU ranges from 47.0 to 54.3 depending on VLM), meaning the reported SOTA numbers partly reflect the strength of a proprietary, closed VLM rather than purely the proposed architecture; reproducibility with the exact same VLM (Gemini 2.5 Pro, API-based) may be difficult given model updates/versioning over time.

The runtime analysis (Table 9, Sec. 8) shows the method takes ~9.25 minutes for a scene with 131 categories, and this scales per-category since each object undergoes independent VLM querying and backward matching (32% of total time); this could scale poorly for scenes with very large numbers of objects/categories compared to embedding-based methods that pay a fixed one-time training cost and then have fast inference at query time.

Text-based semantic hypotheses generated by a VLM (5 nouns per object) are a coarser semantic representation than dense CLIP image embeddings; while the paper argues this improves robustness to viewpoint-based feature inconsistency, it may lose fine-grained visual/textural cues that image embeddings can capture (e.g., color, material subtleties) — the paper does not deeply analyze this potential trade-off with quantitative failure statistics beyond a few qualitative failure examples.

Comparisons are made primarily against the two established benchmarks (LERF, ScanNet); while thorough, both are relatively small-scale/object-centric datasets. Broader scene diversity or larger-scale outdoor/embodied benchmarks are not tested in the main paper (only limited real-world/Grasp-Net qualitative examples without quantitative metrics are given in appendix), limiting generalizability claims somewhat.

The neutral point / entropy thresholding mechanism uses fixed thresholds across all experiments (τ_h=0.9, τ_α=0.1) tuned presumably on LERF; although a sensitivity table is given, it is unclear how robust this choice is to substantially different scene types/densities, and no adaptive or learned alternative is explored.

The method is presented as "training-free," but it still requires online VLM API calls and CLIP text encoding at data-preparation/test time per scene per object, and its performance ceiling is stated to be bounded by "the ongoing evolution of Vision-Language Models" — this dependency somewhat undercuts the framing of an architectural contribution independent of foundation model capability improvements.

Minor: some tables (e.g., Table 2) show the proposed method is not uniformly best on every individual scene/category (e.g., LangSplat/GOI/Occam's LGS/3DVLGS outperform on some LERF scenes such as Teatime/Waldo columns), so the "new SOTA" claim, while true on average, should be stated with this caveat.
